minimize: total cost of the flow on the arcs of a network

solve for:
(a) flow on each arc.

subject to:
(a) flow balance: at each node, flow out minus flow in is its net supply, and no more than it at a supply node;
(b) arc bounds: the flow on each arc is between its lower and upper bound.

assumptions:
(a) cost per unit of flow on each arc is constant;
(b) total supply is at least total demandeach node’s net supply is given: positive at a supply node, negative at a demand node, and zero at a node flow only passes through.

Model 3: Minimum cost network flow

Generalization of Model 2: Transportation and Model 1: Shortest path in Lecture 4.1

Model 3 formulation: Minimum cost network flow

$$
\begin{array}{rlrclll}
& \text{Minimize} & \displaystyle \sum_{k \in E} c_k\, x_k & & & & \\[2pt]
& \text{subject to} & \displaystyle \sum_{k \in E} a_{ik}\, x_k & \le & s_i, & i \in V : s_i > 0 & (a) \\[2pt]
& & \displaystyle \sum_{k \in E} a_{ik}\, x_k & = & s_i, & i \in V : s_i \le 0 & (a) \\[2pt]
& & l_k \;\le\; x_k & \le & u_k, & k \in E & (b)
\end{array}
\tag{4}
$$

Both lines labeled (a) in Eq. 4 are row (a), flow balance, on purpose: the one constraint is written as an inequality at the supply nodes and as an equation at every other node.

where

- $x_k$ = flow on arc $k$ (units)
- $c_k$ = cost per unit of flow on arc $k$ (cost/unit)
- $a_{ik}$ = $\begin{cases} 1, & \text{if arc } k \text{ starts at node } i \\ -1, & \text{if arc } k \text{ ends at node } i \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$
- $s_i$ = net supply of node $i$ (units)
= $\begin{cases} > 0, & \text{supply node } i \\ = 0, & \text{transshipment node } i \\ < 0, & \text{demand node } i \end{cases}$
- $l_k$ = lower bound on the flow on arc $k$, by default $0$ (units)
- $u_k$ = upper bound on the flow on arc $k$, by default $\infty$ (units)
- $V$ = nodes
- $E$ = arcs.

Model 3 states two constraints, and both are rows. Row (a), flow balance, is one row per node, written in two lines: the sum $\sum_k a_{ik} x_k$ is the flow out of node $i$ less the flow into it, which at a supply node can be no more than its supply, and elsewhere must equal the net supply, the negative of a demand at a demand node and zero at a transshipment node. At the supply and demand nodes of a transportation network, row (a) is exactly rows (a) and (b) of Eq. 2, which is why Model 2 is a special case of Model 3. Row (b), arc bounds, is new; with the defaults, $0$ and $\infty$, it is just the nonnegativity of the flows.

Model 3 implementation: Minimum cost network flow

```julia
# Model: minimum cost network flow
# Incidence matrix from an arc list: arc k from i[k] to j[k], +1 where it
# starts and -1 where it ends, one column per arc in the list's order
list2incid(i, j, n) = sparse([i; j], [1:length(i); 1:length(i)],
                             [ones(length(i)); -ones(length(j))],
                             n, length(i))

function mcnf(A, c, s; u = fill(Inf, size(A, 2)), l = zeros(size(A, 2)))
    V, E = 1:size(A, 1), 1:size(A, 2)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    @variable(model, l[k] ≤ x[k ∈ E] ≤ u[k])                  # (b)
    @objective(model, Min, sum(c[k] * x[k] for k ∈ E))
    @constraint(model, supply[i ∈ V; s[i] > 0],
                sum(A[i, k] * x[k] for k ∈ E) ≤ s[i])               # (a)
    @constraint(model, balance[i ∈ V; s[i] ≤ 0],
                sum(A[i, k] * x[k] for k ∈ E) == s[i])              # (a)

    set_silent(model)
    optimize!(model)
    if termination_status(model) == JuMP.OPTIMAL
        return (TC = objective_value(model), x = snapvals(value.(x)))
    end
    error(termination_status(model))
end

```

- 1 sparse(I, J, V, n, m), as in Lecture 2.3, puts V[k] at row I[k] and column J[k] of an $n \times m$ matrix: here the rows are the arcs’ start nodes and then their end nodes, the columns the arc numbers twice, and the values $+1$ and then $-1$. Built from the arc list itself, every arc keeps its own column in the order listed, including the parallel arcs of Ex. 6(d), which a graph built from the same list would merge.
- 2 Row (b) is written as bounds on the variables rather than as constraints: each x[k] lies between its own l[k] and u[k], and an upper bound of Inf is no bound at all.
- 3 The condition after the semicolon keeps only the nodes that meet it: one row (a) for each supply node here, and one for every other node in the balance rows below.

Example 6: Small networks as flows

Solve four small networks as Model 3: the transportation problem of Ex. 4, the shortest path problem of Ex. 1 in Lecture 4.1, the network of Fig. 8 with bounds on its arcs, and the multigraph of Lecture 4.1, Sec. 1, whose cheaper mode between two nodes is capacitated.

Example 6(a): Ex. 4’s transportation problem

Solve Ex. 4’s transportation problem as a minimum cost network flow, and compare the total cost with Ex. 4(b)’s.

In Ex. 4 (Fig. 5), the LP model was created directly from the interlevel matrix C, the matrix of arc costs from one level of nodes to the next, a row for each supply node and a column for each demand node. Since the transportation problem is a special case of the MCNF problem, C can be converted into an incidence matrix, A, and then solved as an MCNF instance.

```julia
# Code block 52: Ex. 4's tableau as an arc list, solved as a network flow
C = [8 6 10 9; 9 12 13 7; 14 9 16 5]
m, n = size(C)
i = repeat(1:m, n)                # supply node of each arc
j = m .+ repeat(1:n, inner = m)   # demand node of each arc
c = vec(C)                        # cost of each arc, column by column
s = [55, 50, 40, -45, -20, -30, -30]
A = list2incid(i, j, m + n)
TCᵒ, xᵒ = mcnf(A, c, s)
@show TCᵒ; reshape(xᵒ, m, n)

```

- 1 vec(C) lists C column by column, so the arcs are listed the same way: supply nodes 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, … and demand nodes 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, …, numbered after the supply nodes. Listed this way, reshape(xᵒ, m, n) returns the flows in the tableau’s layout.

```julia
[u l]
```

Example 6(c): Arc bounds

Solve the network of Fig. 8, then solve it again with an upper bound of 3 on arcs (2,4) and (3,5), an upper bound of 9 on arc (2,5), and a lower bound of 1 on arc (4,5), and compare the two total costs.

Upper and lower arc bounds that differ from the default values of $\infty$ and $0$ can be added to the MCNF LP formulation.

Arc (4,5) is the only arc with a lower-bound $>0$, and arcs (2,4), (2,5), and (3,5) are the only arcs with upper-bounds $<\infty$. In order to provide flexibility with respect to inputting the arc information, the arc list is input as a comma-separated string, where any default upper and lower bounds are not input. This can then be used to create a DataFrame and then the missing default upper and lower bounds can be replaced with their default values.

The arc list, which so far has three columns, the start and end of each arc and its cost, takes the arc bounds as a fourth and a fifth column, the upper bound and then the lower bound. By default an upper bound is infinity and a lower bound is zero, and the columns are needed only for values other than the defaults: an upper bound less than infinity goes in the fourth column and a lower bound greater than zero in the fifth. The upper bound comes fourth and the lower bound last because the lower bound’s default of zero is more often what a problem wants than the upper bound’s of infinity, so a list of four columns leaves every lower bound at zero.

```julia
# Code block 58: the arc list, with its bounds, as a string
using DataFrames, CSV

arclist_str = """
i,j,c,u,l
1,2,2,,
1,3,3,,
2,5,5,9,
2,4,4,3,
3,5,1,3,
4,5,3,,1
"""
println(arclist_str)
arclist_str
```

```text
i,j,c,u,l
1,2,2,,
1,3,3,,
2,5,5,9,
2,4,4,3,
3,5,1,3,
4,5,3,,1

```

```text
"i,j,c,u,l\n1,2,2,,\n1,3,3,,\n2,5,5,9,\n2,4,4,3,\n3,5,1,3,\n4,5,3,,1\n"
```

```julia
# Code block 59: the string read into a DataFrame
df = CSV.read(IOBuffer(arclist_str), DataFrame)
prt(string.(df))

```

- 1 IOBuffer makes the string read like a file, so CSV.read parses it into a DataFrame as it would a .csv file on disk.
- 2 Each empty field of the string is read as missing, which Code block 60 fills. prt cannot yet print a missing in a table of numbers, so string. turns every entry into text first; df itself keeps its numbers.

```text
  i  j  c        u        l
───────────────────────────
  1  2  2  missing  missing
  1  3  3  missing  missing
  2  5  5        9  missing
  2  4  4        3  missing
  3  5  1        3  missing
  4  5  3  missing        1
```

Code block 60 fills the empty bounds with their defaults using coalesce, used in Lecture 2.5, Sec. 7 for imputing missing data: coalesce.(x, v) replaces each missing in x with v and leaves every other value as it is, so an upper bound left empty becomes Inf and a lower bound left empty becomes 0.

```julia
# Code block 60: the default bounds filled in
df.u = coalesce.(df.u, Inf) # Replace missing values in 'u' with infinity
df.l = coalesce.(df.l, 0)   # Replace missing values in 'l' with zero
prt(df)
```

```text
4  2  4  4    3  0
5  3  5  1    3  0
6  4  5  3  Inf  1
```

```text
────────────────────────────────
1  1  2  2  Inf  0   3         0
2  1  3  3  Inf  0   3         6
3  2  5  5    9  0   4         2
```

Without bounds, all six of node 1’s units take the path 1 → 3 → 5 at 4 per unit, and node 2’s two units take arc (2,5). The upper bound of 3 on arc (3,5) halves the cheap path’s flow, so node 1’s other three units go by way of node 2; the lower bound of 1 on arc (4,5) forces one unit onto the costlier 2 → 4 → 5; and the total rises from 34 to 45. Bounds can only add constraints, so the total with them can be no less than without them: the Bounds check of Lecture 1.2, passed.

With its bounds, the five-node network’s least total cost is 45, against 34 without them

Example 6(d): A capacitated mode

In the multigraph of Fig. 4 in Lecture 4.1, nodes 1, 2 and 3 supply 30, 10 and 20 units, and nodes 4 and 5 demand 40 and 20. The cheaper of the two modes between nodes 1 and 4, at a cost of 6 per unit, can carry at most 20 units; the other, at 18, is uncapacitated. Determine the least-cost flows, with and without the capacity.

Of the two arcs between nodes 1 and 4, the 18, at the higher cost, might represent a more costly mode of transport, and the 6 a less costly one with limited capacity, so that only so much flow can use the cheaper mode, and beyond that quantity the higher-cost arc is needed. Representing that takes upper and lower bounds on the arcs. So there are contexts where a multigraph is wanted, and when it is, the arc list has to be used, since the adjacency matrix cannot represent it. That is one of the reasons for having several representations of a network: some cannot represent everything, and in other cases one is simply more convenient than another, as the adjacency matrix often is, even though it cannot represent everything.

Fig. 11 draws the multigraph of Lecture 4.1 with the net supplies and the capacity of this example:

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
# Code block 63: Ex. 6(d)'s multigraph, drawn with Code block 50
# The nodes where Lecture 4.1 draws them; each two-way pair of arcs 1-4
# drawn as one arc with a head at each end
XYm = [(0.0, 2.0), (0.0, 1.0), (0.0, 0.0), (2.4, 1.6), (2.4, 0.4)]
drawnet(XYm, [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3], [4, 4, 5, 4, 5, 5, 5],
        ["6, 20", "18", "10", "0", "13", "16", "3"],
        [30, 10, 20, -40, -20]; off = [0.07, -0.07, 0, 0, 0, 0.07, -0.07],
        two = [true, true, false, false, false, false, false],
        at = [0.5, 0.5, 0.2, 0.3, 0.3, 0.5, 0.5],
        side = [1, -1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1],
        w = 400, h = 330, lim = ((-0.7, 3.1), (-0.4, 2.4)))
```

Figure 11: Lecture 4.1’s multigraph as a minimum cost network flow, each node labeled with its net supply: nodes 1, 2 and 3 (red) supply 30, 10 and 20 units, and nodes 4 and 5 (green) demand 40 and 20. Each arc is labeled with its cost per unit. The two two-way arcs between nodes 1 and 4 are the two modes, and the cheaper’s label, 6, 20, gives its cost per unit and the 20 units it can carry from node 1 to node 4.

```julia
# Code block 64: Lecture 4.1's multigraph, from its arc list, as a flow
i = [1, 4, 1, 4, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3]     # two-way arcs 1-4 listed both ways
j = [4, 1, 4, 1, 5, 4, 5, 5, 5]
c = [6, 6, 18, 18, 10, 0, 13, 16, 3]
s = [30, 10, 20, -40, -20]
u = [20, Inf, Inf, Inf, Inf, Inf, Inf, Inf, Inf]   # cheap mode 1 -> 4
A = list2incid(i, j, length(s))
TCᵒwoBnds, xᵒwoBnds = mcnf(A, c, s)
TCᵒ, xᵒ = mcnf(A, c, s; u = u)
@show TCᵒ
@show TCᵒwoBnds
prt([i j c u xᵒwoBnds xᵒ]; row_title = "Arc",
    cols = ["From", "To", "Cost", "Capacity", "Uncapped", "Capped"])
```

```text
TCᵒ = 360.0
TCᵒwoBnds = 240.0
Arc  From  To  Cost  Capacity  Uncapped  Capped
───────────────────────────────────────────────
  1     1   4     6        20        30      20
  2     4   1     6       Inf         0       0
  3     1   4    18       Inf         0      10
  4     4   1    18       Inf         0       0
  5     1   5    10       Inf         0       0
  6     2   4     0       Inf        10      10
  7     2   5    13       Inf         0       0
  8     3   5    16       Inf         0       0
  9     3   5     3       Inf        20      20
```

The arc list is the one Lecture 4.1 draws as Fig. 4 in Lecture 4.1, as it stands, the parallel arcs 1 → 4 at 6 and at 18 each a row of their own, and the arc of cost 0 from node 2 to node 4 kept as it is. Uncapacitated, all 30 of node 1’s units take the cheaper mode, for a total of 240. Capacitated, the cheaper mode carries its 20 and the costlier one the other 10, for 360: the costlier mode is used only for the flow the cheaper one cannot carry. An adjacency matrix could hold only one of the two arcs from 1 to 4, and so could not pose this problem at all.

With the cheaper mode capacitated at 20 units, the least total cost is 360, against 240 uncapacitated

Example 7: Earthquake emergency response

Determine the least-cost flows, as Model 3, that deliver the 700 pallets the Field Hospital needs through the relief network of Table 6; if the network as it stands cannot deliver them, determine which arc’s capacity to raise, and the least total cost with it.

A major earthquake has struck a region, and emergency medical supplies must be transported to a central field hospital. Two warehouses have supplies, but the routes are compromised, with varying costs, travel risks, and transportation capacities. The goal is to meet the hospital’s demand at the lowest possible cost. The relief effort’s logistics network is composed of six key locations, as shown in Table 5. The supply originates from two source nodes: the Regional Warehouse (RW), which holds 500 pallets of general supplies, and a Specialty Pharmacy (SP) with 200 pallets of critical medicines. From these points, supplies travel through three transshipment nodes: a Local Airfield (LA) for consolidation, a Central Distribution Hub (CH) for sorting, and a Staging Area (SA) for final preparation. The ultimate goal is to deliver the combined 700 pallets to the single demand node, the Field Hospital (FH), to make it fully operational.

Table 5: The relief network’s nodes, each with its net supply: positive at a supply node, zero at a transshipment node and negative at the demand node.

| Node | Name | Type | Net supply |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Regional Warehouse (RW) | Supply | 500 |
| 2 | Specialty Pharmacy (SP) | Supply | 200 |
| 3 | Local Airfield (LA) | Transshipment | 0 |
| 4 | Central Distribution Hub (CH) | Transshipment | 0 |
| 5 | Staging Area (SA) | Transshipment | 0 |
| 6 | Field Hospital (FH) | Demand | $-700$ |

Table 6: The relief network’s arcs, each with its cost per pallet and the least and the most it can carry.

| From Node | To Node | Cost (\$/pallet) | Lower Bound (pallets) | Upper Bound (pallets) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (RW) | 3 (LA) | 4 | 0 | 400 | Main road, limited trucks |
| 1 (RW) | 4 (CH) | 6 | 0 | 300 | Secondary road, some damage |
| 2 (SP) | 4 (CH) | 3 | 0 | 200 | Direct, efficient route |
| 3 (LA) | 5 (SA) | 10 | 0 | 150 | Expensive helicopter transport |
| 4 (CH) | 5 (SA) | 5 | 100 | 600 | Main convoy, needs scarce escort detail |
| 5 (SA) | 6 (FH) | 2 | 0 | 800 | Secure final-mile shuttle |

The arcs are entered as Ex. 6(c)’s were, an arc list in a string, the empty lower bounds read as missing and set to zero, and the net supplies are those of Table 5:

```julia
# Code block 65: the relief network's arcs, with their bounds, as a flow
arclist_str = """
i,j,c,u,l
1,3,4,400,
1,4,6,300,
2,4,3,200,
3,5,10,150,
4,5,5,600,100
5,6,2,800,
"""
df = CSV.read(IOBuffer(arclist_str), DataFrame)
df.l = coalesce.(df.l, 0)
s = [500, 200, 0, 0, 0, -700]
A = list2incid(df.i, df.j, length(s))
prt(df)
```

```text
   i  j   c    u    l
─────────────────────
1  1  3   4  400    0
2  1  4   6  300    0
3  2  4   3  200    0
4  3  5  10  150    0
5  4  5   5  600  100
6  5  6   2  800    0
```

Since this problem has restrictive upper bounds, there is a significant probability that it may not be feasible to satisfy the required demand. As a result, the call to mcnf, the implementation of Model 3, is wrapped so that its error, which names the solver’s status, is printed rather than stopping the script.

```julia
# Code block 66: the network as it stands
try
    mcnf(A, df.c, s; u = df.u, l = df.l)
catch e
    showerror(stdout, e)
end
```

```text
INFEASIBLE
```

Since the model is infeasible, likely due to the upper bounds on flows being too restrictive, one way to look at this is to examine the network structure, where the label on each arc gives its cost and its bounds (Fig. 12).

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
# Code block 67: the relief network, drawn with Code block 50
XYq = [(0.0, 1.9), (0.0, 0.3), (1.4, 2.2), (1.4, 0.6), (2.8, 1.3),
       (4.2, 1.3)]
drawnet(XYq, df.i, df.j, arclab.(df.c, df.u, df.l), s;
        roles = ["RW", "SP", "LA", "CH", "SA", "FH"], rotate = true,
        dirs = [180, 180, 90, 270, 270, 0], side = [1, -1, -1, 1, -1, 1],
        legend = (3.5, 2.4), w = 600, h = 330,
        lim = ((-0.8, 5.0), (-0.4, 2.8)))
```

Figure 12: The relief network of Ex. 7, each node labeled with its name and its net supply: the Regional Warehouse (RW) and the Specialty Pharmacy (SP) supply 500 and 200 pallets, the Field Hospital (FH) needs 700, and the airfield (LA), the hub (CH) and the staging area (SA) are transshipment nodes. Each arc is labeled $c, u, l$: its cost per pallet, its upper bound and its lower bound, a default left off the end, as the key at the top right reads.

In looking at the graph, at most 500 units can flow into Node 4 and then on to Node 5. Since only 150 units can travel from 3 to 5, the total of 650 is less than the required demand of 700 at Node 6. One way to fix this is to “somehow try to” increase the capacity between 3 and 5 to 200.

```julia
# Code block 68: the helicopter's capacity, arc (3,5), raised to 200
df2 = deepcopy(df) # deepcopy used so that `df2` changes don't change `df`
df2.u[4] = 200
prt(df2)
```

```text
   i  j   c    u    l
─────────────────────
1  1  3   4  400    0
2  1  4   6  300    0
3  2  4   3  200    0
4  3  5  10  200    0
5  4  5   5  600  100
6  5  6   2  800    0
```

```julia
# Code block 69: the network with it
TC2ᵒ, x2ᵒ = mcnf(A, df2.c, s; u = df2.u, l = df2.l)
@show TC2ᵒ; x2ᵒ
```

```text
TC2ᵒ = 9100.0
```

```text
6-element Vector{Float64}:
 200.0
 300.0
 200.0
 200.0
 500.0
 700.0
```

Feasible now. But this was achieved by increasing the expensive helicopter capacity. Another possibility is to “somehow try to” increase the capacity between 1 and 4 to 350. At a cost of \$6 per unit, increasing this by 50 is cheaper than increasing the expensive \$10 per unit helicopter capacity by 50.

```julia
# Code block 70: road (1,4)'s capacity raised to 350 instead
df3 = deepcopy(df)
df3.u[2] = 350
prt(df3)
```

```text
   i  j   c    u    l
─────────────────────
1  1  3   4  400    0
2  1  4   6  350    0
3  2  4   3  200    0
4  3  5  10  150    0
5  4  5   5  600  100
6  5  6   2  800    0
```

```julia
# Code block 71: the network with it
TC3ᵒ, x3ᵒ = mcnf(A, df3.c, s; u = df3.u, l = df3.l)
@show TC3ᵒ; x3ᵒ
```

```text
TC3ᵒ = 8950.0
```

```text
6-element Vector{Float64}:
 150.0
 350.0
 200.0
 150.0
 550.0
 700.0
```

Raising road (1,4) instead delivers all 700 pallets for 8,950, 150 less than raising the helicopter’s: the 50 pallets the path 1 → 3 → 5 carried at 4 + 10 = 14 a pallet go by road, 1 → 4 → 5, at 6 + 5 = 11, a saving of 3 × 50 = 150, the Triangulate check of Lecture 1.2. The count before Code block 68, at most 650 pallets into node 5 against the 700 needed, is the Bounds check: it explains the infeasibility without the linear program.

As the network stands, no flow delivers the 700 pallets; raising road (1,4)’s capacity to 350 delivers them at a least total cost of 8,950, against 9,100 by raising the helicopter’s to 200
